title: Reported statement: said that
plainEnglish: It relays what someone else said as a statement, like English said that.
whenToUse: Reach for this whenever you are the messenger passing on someone's words: relaying a boss's announcement (팀장님이 회의 늦어진다고 했어요 = the team lead said the meeting is delayed), repeating gossip (걔가 너 좋아한다고 하던데? = word is she likes you), texting a plan a friend told you, or quoting a sign or notice. The intent is to mark the content as not-mine-but-reported, which lets you stay neutral about whether it's true. It also works for relaying your OWN earlier words (제가 안 간다고 했잖아요 = I told you I'm not going). In casual storytelling Koreans often swap 했어요 for -다고 하더라고요 (I heard that…) or even drop the 하다 entirely (걔가 바쁘대 = she says she's busy), but the core -다고 chunk stays the same.
attachmentRule: For a present-tense verb add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel stem (가다→간다고) and -는다고 after a consonant stem (먹다→먹는다고). Adjectives and 있다/없다 just add -다고 (춥다→춥다고, 재미있다→재미있다고). Past tense uses -았/었다고 (갔다고, 먹었다고). A noun takes -(이)라고 (학생이라고, 친구라고). 하다 is usually said as 했어요 (said) or 한다고/하더라고 in retelling.
contrastWith: The trap is mixing up the three reporting endings by sentence type. Use -다고 하다 ONLY for a plain statement (비 온다고 했어요 = said it's raining); switch to -냐고 하다 for a relayed question (비 오냐고 물어봤어요 = asked if it's raining) and to -(으)라고 하다 for a relayed command (빨리 오라고 했어요 = told me to come quickly). A second confusion is -다고 하다 vs the surprised/disagreeing -다고? as a standalone reply (뭐? 안 온다고? = What? You're not coming?). Match the ending to the original sentence's punctuation: period→-다고, question mark→-냐고, exclamation/imperative→-(으)라고.

examples.ko: 엄마가 일찍 자라고… 아니, 일찍 잔다고 했어요.
examples.en: Mom said she's going to bed early.
examples.note: Plain statement = -ㄴ다고; here 자다→잔다고 because the stem ends in a vowel.

examples.en: The team lead said the meeting will be 30 minutes late.
examples.note: 하셨어요 honorifies the boss who spoke; the reported verb 늦어진다고 stays plain.

examples.ko: 걔가 어제 그 카페 진짜 맛있었다고 했어.
examples.en: She said that cafe was really good yesterday.
examples.note: Past report uses -았/었다고: 맛있다→맛있었다고, and 했어 is casual 반말.

examples.ko: 집주인이 다음 달부터 월세 올린다고 했어요.
examples.en: The landlord said he'll raise the rent starting next month.
examples.note: 올리다→올린다고: a real-life situation where you relay bad news you received.

commonMistakes: Gluing -다고 onto the polite form, like 가요고 하다. WHY it's wrong: indirect speech strips the speech level off the inner sentence and uses the plain dictionary-style ending. FIX: 간다고 해요, never 가요고 해요.
Forgetting the verb-vs-adjective split: saying 춥는다고 for an adjective. WHY: only verbs take -ㄴ다고/-는다고; adjectives and 있다/없다 take bare -다고. FIX: 춥다고, 재미있다고, not 춥는다고.
Reporting a yes/no question with -다고, e.g. 시간 있다고 물어봤어요 to mean asked if I have time. WHY: that says they STATED they have time. FIX: 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend said he is coming tomorrow.
She said the food was delicious. (past)
The boss said he is busy.

studyOrder: Decide if the relayed sentence is a verb, adjective, or noun
Verbs: add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel, -는다고 after a consonant
Adjectives and 있다/없다: just add -다고; nouns add -(이)라고
Finish with 하다, usually 했어요 to mean someone said
beginnerExplanation: V-다고 하다 is how Korean relays what someone said, the way English uses said that. Mnemonic: think of -다고 as putting the other person's words inside invisible quotation marks, and 하다 as the verb saying. But before the quote marks go on, the sentence must take off its polite shoes — that is, drop the -요 and stand in plain form — so 가요 becomes 간다고, and 먹어요 becomes 먹는다고. Adjectives are easier and simply add -다고, as in 피곤하다고 (said she is tired), and past tense for everything is -았/었다고 (맛있었다고). You'll hear this constantly: 팀장님이 회의 늦는다고 했어요 passes on the boss's message, and 친구가 내일 온다고 했어요 reports a friend's plan. The number one beginner slip is leaving the polite shoes on — 가요고 해요 — so drill it as 간다고 해요.

title: Reported question: asked whether
plainEnglish: It relays a question that someone else asked, like English asked whether or asked if.
whenToUse: Use this to pass along a question someone fired at you or at a third person: recounting a job interview (면접관이 왜 지원했냐고 물어봤어요 = the interviewer asked why I applied), telling a friend what your mom interrogated you about, or reporting a crush's probing question (여자친구 있냐고 물어봤어 = asked if I have a girlfriend). The intent is to report the asking event, not to ask the listener anything yourself, so the listener doesn't have to answer. It naturally pairs with the warm verb 물어보다 (to try asking) in 물어봤어요, which sounds friendlier than the blunter 물었어요. For relaying a wh-question you keep the question word inside: 어디 가냐고 (asked where I'm going), 누구냐고 (asked who it is).
attachmentRule: In everyday speech add -냐고 to the plain stem of verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike (가냐고, 먹냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고). Past tense uses -았/었냐고 (갔냐고, 먹었냐고). A noun takes -(이)냐고 (학생이냐고, 누구냐고). The reporting verb is usually 물어봤어요 (asked) or 했어요. The fuller written forms 가느냐고/먹느냐고 also exist but sound stiff in speech.
contrastWith: The sharp line is -냐고 하다 (reports a QUESTION) vs -다고 하다 (reports a STATEMENT). Compare 시간 있냐고 했어요 (asked if I have time) with 시간 있다고 했어요 (said that he has time) — same words, opposite meaning, decided purely by 냐 vs 다. A second, subtler contrast is -냐고 하다 vs the embedded-question -는지 (시간 있는지 물어봤어요 also works and is a touch softer/more indirect); -냐고 reproduces the question more directly, almost like air-quoting it, while -는지 frames it as wondering. Rule of thumb: if the original ended in a question mark, you need -냐고.

examples.en: My friend asked if I have time this weekend.
examples.note: 있다 takes plain -냐고 → 있냐고; 물어봤어요 is the natural reporting verb.

examples.en: My mom asked whether I had eaten.
examples.note: Past question = -았/었냐고: 먹다→먹었냐고; 하셨어요 honorifies mom.

examples.en: The girl I'm into asked me if I have a girlfriend.
examples.note: 나한테 marks who was asked; 반말 ending 물어봤어 fits casual gossip.

examples.ko: 면접관이 왜 우리 회사에 지원했냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.en: The interviewer asked why I applied to our company.
examples.note: A wh-question keeps 왜 inside the report; 지원하다→지원했냐고 (past).

commonMistakes: Using -다고 for a relayed question, e.g. 시간 있다고 물어봤어요. WHY: -다고 reports a statement, so this oddly says they 'stated' something while 'asking'. FIX: 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요.
Keeping the polite -요 before -냐고, like 가요냐고. WHY: indirect speech uses the plain stem, not the listener-level form. FIX: 가냐고, not 가요냐고.
Adding the verb ending -는 to an adjective, like 바쁘는냐고. WHY: spoken -냐고 attaches the same way to adjectives with no -는-. FIX: 바쁘냐고.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend asked if I'm coming.
He asked if it was expensive. (past)
She asked who that person is.

studyOrder: Confirm the original sentence was a question
Add -냐고 to the plain stem of the verb or adjective
Use -았/었냐고 for past and -(이)냐고 for nouns
Finish with 물어봤어요 or 했어요 to mean someone asked
beginnerExplanation: V-냐고 하다 relays a question that someone asked, matching English asked if or asked whether. Mnemonic: the syllable 냐 is the squashed sound of a spoken question (가? → 가냐?), so 냐고 = the question, frozen and handed to you. The big convenience is that modern spoken Korean uses this one ending for verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike, so 가냐고 (asked if I go), 바쁘냐고 (asked if I'm busy), and 시간 있냐고 (asked if I have time) all work the same way. Past questions use -았/었냐고, as in 밥 먹었냐고 했어요 (asked whether I ate). The reporting verb is most naturally 물어봤어요, literally tried asking, which sounds warm and conversational. Beginners often reuse -다고 here, but that ending is only for statements; if the original had a question mark, switch to -냐고 — so 여자친구 있냐고 물어봤어, not 있다고.

title: Worried that / afraid that
plainEnglish: It says you do something because you are worried or afraid that an unwanted thing might happen.
whenToUse: Use this to give the anxious reason behind a precaution you take: leaving early because you fear traffic (길 막힐까 봐 일찍 나왔어요), packing an umbrella in case it rains (비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요), texting twice because you worry you were ignored. The pattern frames the action as defensive — you act to head off a bad outcome. It commonly leads into 걱정이에요 / 무서워요 / 긴장돼요 to name the feeling (떨어질까 봐 긴장돼요 = nervous I'll fail), or into a past precaution you already took. Literally it comes from -ㄹ까 (I wonder if…) + 보다 (to see/suppose), so the feel is 'supposing the bad thing might happen, …'. Don't use it for hopeful or neutral wondering — only when the imagined result is unwanted.
attachmentRule: Add -ㄹ까 봐 to a vowel-ending stem (가다→갈까 봐, 오다→올까 봐) and -을까 봐 to a consonant-ending stem (늦다→늦을까 봐, 먹다→먹을까 봐). For a worry about something already past, use -았/었을까 봐 (실수했을까 봐). The main clause is your reaction, often ending in a past action you took. The full form 봐요 is more polite; 봐 is casual.
contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 gives a WORRIED reason, while -(으)니까 gives a neutral, factual reason. Compare 비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요 (packed an umbrella fearing it might rain — it may or may not rain) with 비 오니까 우산 챙겼어요 (it's raining, so I packed one — rain is a fact). A second contrast is -(으)ㄹ까 봐 vs -지 않게/-(으)ㄹ까 봐 the purpose marker -도록: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 fronts the fear, whereas 늦지 않도록 fronts the goal. If there's no genuine dread of a bad result, -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is the wrong tool.

examples.ko: 늦을까 봐 한 시간 일찍 나왔어요.
examples.en: I left an hour early because I was worried I'd be late.
examples.note: Consonant stem 늦다 → -을까 봐; the main clause is the precaution you took.

examples.en: I'm so nervous because I'm afraid I'll fail the interview.
examples.note: Here the worry leads into a FEELING (긴장돼요), not an action.

examples.en: I kept checking because I was afraid my message had been left on read.
examples.note: Worry about a PAST event uses -았/었을까 봐: 씹히다→씹혔을까 봐.

examples.en: I packed an umbrella in case it rains.
examples.note: Vowel stem 오다 → -ㄹ까 봐; classic 'just in case' use about an uncertain future.

commonMistakes: Using it for a neutral reason instead of a worry, like 배고플까 봐 먹어요 to just mean because I'm hungry. WHY: there's no dreaded outcome — being hungry isn't a feared event. FIX: 배고프니까 먹어요.
Forgetting the consonant linker -을-, e.g. 늦까 봐. WHY: a consonant stem needs the -을- bridge before ㄹ까. FIX: 늦을까 봐.
Putting the main-clause precaution in the future when it already happened, e.g. 늦을까 봐 일찍 나갈 거예요 to describe what you did. WHY: the precaution is usually a completed action. FIX: 늦을까 봐 일찍 나왔어요.

practiceItems.prompt: I left early because I was worried I'd be late.
I packed extra because I was afraid it wouldn't be enough.

studyOrder: Identify the bad outcome you are worried about
Add -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel or -을까 봐 after a consonant
Use -았/었을까 봐 if the worry is about something past
State the action you took in the main clause
beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐 is the phrase Koreans use when worry drives an action, roughly worried that or afraid that. Analogy: it's the little 'what if…' that pushes you to grab an umbrella — 비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요 literally lines up as 'what if it rains? → so I packed an umbrella.' The structure is worry first, action second: 지각할까 봐 택시 탔어요 means I took a taxi because I was afraid I'd be late. Attachment is the usual split, -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel and -을까 봐 after a consonant, so 늦다 becomes 늦을까 봐. The key feeling is dread of a bad result, which separates it from the neutral reason marker -(으)니까; you wouldn't say 배고플까 봐 just to explain you're hungry. In casual texting you'll see the short 봐, but 봐요 sounds more polite to someone senior.

title: It seems / I think
plainEnglish: It softens a statement into a guess or impression, like English it seems or I think.
whenToUse: Use this to hedge — to offer an opinion, guess, or read on a situation without sounding too sure: judging from evidence (길이 젖었네, 비 왔던 것 같아요 = roads are wet, seems it rained), giving a gentle opinion (이 영화 좀 별로인 것 같아요 = I kinda think this movie isn't great), or predicting (배달 늦을 것 같아요 = I think the delivery will be late). The intent is social softness: flat assertions can feel pushy in Korean, so wrapping your claim in 것 같다 makes you sound modest and considerate. It's also handy for talking about your OWN feelings politely (저는 괜찮은 것 같아요 = I think I'm fine with it). Heard constantly in cafes, offices, and reviews.
attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 것 같다 (가다→가는 것 같다, 먹다→먹는 것 같다). For a present adjective add -은 것 같다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 것 같다 after a vowel (춥다→추운 것 같다, 크다→큰 것 같다). Past uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (간 것 같다, 먹은 것 같다) and future uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (갈 것 같다). 것 is often spoken as 거, giving 가는 거 같아요.
contrastWith: -는 것 같다 is a soft, evidence-based personal guess, while the suffix -겠- is a more immediate, gut-feeling inference (맛있겠다! = that looks delicious! — instant reaction) and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 leans toward a prediction about the future (비 올 것 같아요 = looks like it'll rain). A second, important contrast is -는 것 같다 vs -는 척하다: 자는 것 같다 = it genuinely SEEMS she's asleep (your honest guess), whereas 자는 척하다 = she's PRETENDING to sleep (deliberate fakery). Same modifier shape, totally different worlds — honest impression vs put-on act.

examples.ko: 이 카페 사람이 너무 많은 것 같아요.
examples.en: This cafe seems to have too many people.
examples.note: Adjective 많다 → -은 것 같다 (많은 것 같다), softening a complaint politely.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 좀 바쁜 것 같아.
examples.en: She seems kind of busy these days.
examples.note: Adjective 바쁘다 → 바쁜 것 같아 (반말); never 바쁘는 것 같다.

examples.ko: 어제 비 온 것 같아요. 길이 다 젖었어요.
examples.en: It seems it rained yesterday. The roads are all wet.
examples.note: PAST inference uses -(으)ㄴ: 오다→온 것 같다, guessing from evidence.

examples.en: I think the delivery is going to be a bit late.
examples.note: FUTURE guess uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다: 늦다→늦을 것 같다 (a prediction).

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 것 같다 on an adjective, like 바쁘는 것 같다. WHY: -는- modifies verbs only; adjectives take -은/-ㄴ. FIX: 바쁜 것 같다.

Mixing up the tense modifier: saying 가는 것 같다 when you mean 'seems to have gone.' WHY: -는 is present (seems to go), -(으)ㄴ is past (간 것 같다 = seems to have gone). FIX: pick the modifier by the time you mean.
Overusing 것 같다 for things you actually know for sure, e.g. 제 이름은 민수인 것 같아요. WHY: hedging a certain fact sounds oddly unsure of your own name. FIX: just say 제 이름은 민수예요.

practiceItems.prompt: It seems like it's going to rain. (future)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
Pick the tense: present, past -(으)ㄴ, or future -(으)ㄹ
Build the right modifier, e.g. 가는 / 간 / 갈
Add 것 같다 (or spoken 거 같아요) to mean it seems
beginnerExplanation: A/V-는 것 같다 is the everyday way Koreans soften what they say into a guess, like it seems or I think. Analogy: 것 means 'thing/the fact,' and 같다 means 'is like,' so the whole frame is 'it's like the thing where ___' — a gentle 'feels like' wrapper around your claim. It's everywhere because stating things too bluntly can sound arrogant, so 그 식당 닫은 것 같아요 (it seems the place is closed) feels kinder than a flat assertion. The form rides Korean's modifier endings: present verbs use -는 (가는 것 같다), present adjectives use -은/-ㄴ (바쁜 것 같다), past uses -(으)ㄴ (간 것 같다), future uses -(으)ㄹ (올 것 같다). In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거, so you'll hear 가는 거 같아요. Two pitfalls: don't put -는 on an adjective, and watch the tense modifier, since 가는 것 같다 and 간 것 같다 mean different things.

title: Decide to / agree to
plainEnglish: It says you decided or agreed to do something, often a plan with yourself or others.
whenToUse: Use this to announce a settled decision or a mutual agreement: a New Year's resolution (올해는 운동하기로 했어요 = I've decided to work out this year), a plan locked in with friends (우리 주말에 만나기로 했어요 = we decided to meet this weekend), a couple's or team's arrangement (매주 금요일에 회의하기로 했어요). The intent is to report a choice that's already been made and agreed on, so it almost always surfaces in the past as -기로 했어요. For a firmer 'I made up my mind' nuance, upgrade to -기로 마음먹었어요 or -기로 결심했어요. It frequently sets up a contrast with reality (가기로 했는데 못 갔어요 = we'd decided to go but couldn't). It's about plans and resolutions, not about promising the listener directly in the moment.
attachmentRule: Attach -기로 하다 to the plain verb stem with no vowel or consonant change at all (가다→가기로 하다, 먹다→먹기로 하다, 운동하다→운동하기로 하다). The decision is usually reported in the past as -기로 했어요 (decided), since the choice is already made. To express a firm resolution you can say -기로 마음먹었어요. Negative is -지 않기로 하다 (안 가기로 했어요).
contrastWith: -기로 하다 marks a settled decision/agreement already made, while -(으)ㄹ게요 is an on-the-spot promise to the listener (지금 갈게요 = I'll go now, said as you commit). Compare 내일 갈게요 (I promise you I'll go tomorrow) with 내일 가기로 했어요 (it's been decided/arranged that I go tomorrow). A second contrast is -기로 하다 vs the simple intention -(으)려고 하다: -(으)려고 하다 = I'm planning/intending to (still soft, could change), whereas -기로 했어요 = it's locked in, a firm decision. Use -기로 했어요 to report a plan you've nailed down.

examples.en: I decided to quit smoking starting this year.
examples.note: Plain stem + -기로 했어요; a solo resolution reported in the past.

examples.en: We decided to meet at the Han River this weekend.
examples.note: 우리 signals a MUTUAL agreement — the most common use of -기로 하다.

examples.ko: 돈 모으려고 당분간 택시 안 타기로 했어.
examples.en: To save money, I decided not to take taxis for a while.
examples.note: Negative decision: 안 + verb + -기로 했어 (= 타지 않기로 했어).

examples.ko: 같이 가기로 했는데 걔가 갑자기 취소했어요.
examples.en: We'd decided to go together but she suddenly canceled.
examples.note: -기로 했는데 sets up the decision, then reality breaks it.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기로, like 가아기로 하다 or 먹어기로 하다. WHY: -기로 always attaches to the bare stem, no -아/어. FIX: 가기로 하다, 먹기로 하다.
Using present 하다 for a decision already settled, e.g. 만나기로 해요 to mean 'we decided to meet.' WHY: a finished decision is reported in the past. FIX: 만나기로 했어요.
Putting the negative in the wrong spot, like 가기로 안 했어요 to mean 'decided not to go.' WHY: that means 'didn't decide to go.' FIX: 안 가기로 했어요 / 가지 않기로 했어요.

practiceItems.prompt: We decided to meet next week.

studyOrder: Identify the action you decided on
Take the plain verb stem with no change
Add -기로 하다, usually as -기로 했어요
For a negative decision use -지 않기로 or 안 ...-기로
beginnerExplanation: V-기로 하다 is how you announce a decision or an agreed plan, and it's pleasantly regular because you just add -기로 하다 to the bare verb stem — no spelling changes. Mnemonic: -기 turns the verb into a noun-y 'the doing of it,' and -로 is 'toward/as,' so -기로 하다 ≈ 'I set things up toward doing it' = I've decided to do it. Because a decision is normally already made by the time you mention it, the natural form is past -기로 했어요: 우리 다음 주에 만나기로 했어요 = we decided to meet next week; 담배 끊기로 했어요 = I decided to quit smoking. It fits solo resolutions and group agreements equally. For a decision NOT to do something, slot the negative in front: 안 가기로 했어요 or 가지 않기로 했어요. Keep it apart from -(으)ㄹ게요, which is a promise you make to someone right now; -기로 했어요 reports a plan you already locked in.

title: Pretend to / act like
plainEnglish: It says someone pretends or fakes doing or being something.
whenToUse: Use this for putting on an act — faking a state or action that isn't real: looking busy when the boss walks by (일하는 척했어요), dodging an awkward encounter (전 남친 보고 못 본 척했어 = saw my ex and pretended not to), feigning illness to skip something (아픈 척했어요), or playing dumb (모르는 척하다 = act like you don't know). The intent is deliberate deception or face-saving, often a little comedic or sly, so it shows up constantly in stories about work, dating, and social escapes. It commonly pairs with the imperative 척하지 마 (don't pretend) when you call someone out. The literary equivalent 체하다 means the same thing. Note it implies the speaker KNOWS it's fake.
attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 척하다 (자다→자는 척하다, 먹다→먹는 척하다). For an adjective add -은 척하다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 척하다 after a vowel (아프다→아픈 척하다, 바쁘다→바쁜 척하다). Past action uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (안 들은 척하다 = pretend not to have heard). You may also see 체하다, which means the same thing.
contrastWith: -는 척하다 = deliberately FAKING something untrue, while -는 것 같다 = it HONESTLY seems true to you (a genuine guess). The pair 자는 척하다 (pretending to sleep — they're awake) vs 자는 것 같다 (seems to be asleep — your honest read) shows the gulf: intentional act vs sincere impression. A second contrast is -는 척하다 vs -는 듯이 (모르는 척했다 = pretended not to know, full-on act; 모르는 듯이 행동했다 = behaved as if not knowing, more 'in the manner of'). When the point is conscious pretense aimed at fooling someone, -는 척하다 is the word.

examples.en: My boss came so I pretended to be working hard.
examples.note: Present verb 일하다 → -는 척하다; the universal office survival line.

examples.ko: 전 남친 마주쳤는데 그냥 못 본 척했어.
examples.en: I ran into my ex but I just pretended not to see him.
examples.note: Completed action uses -(으)ㄴ: 보다→못 본 척했어 (pretended not to have seen).

examples.en: I pretended to be sick to skip the company dinner.
examples.note: Adjective 아프다 → 아픈 척했어요; never 아프는 척하다.

examples.en: She totally knows but acts like she doesn't, you know.
examples.note: 모르다→모르는 척; -잖아 nudges shared knowledge ('you know how she is').

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 척하다 on an adjective, like 아프는 척하다. WHY: adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 척하다, not -는-. FIX: 아픈 척하다.
Confusing it with -는 것 같다, e.g. saying 자는 것 같다 when you mean someone is faking. WHY: 것 같다 is an honest guess, not pretense. FIX: 자는 척하다 for deliberate faking.
Using present -는 척 for an action already completed, e.g. 안 듣는 척했어요 to mean 'pretended not to have heard it.' WHY: a finished action needs the past modifier. FIX: 안 들은 척했어요.

practiceItems.prompt: I pretended not to hear. (past action)

Verbs: present -는 척, past action -(으)ㄴ 척
Adjectives: -은 척 after a consonant, -ㄴ 척 after a vowel
Add 척하다 and conjugate it for your tense
beginnerExplanation: V-는 척하다 means to pretend or fake, and it shows up a lot in stories about work, dating, and saving face. Mnemonic: 척 is the 'putting on a show' word, so V-는 척하다 = 'do the show of V-ing.' The form uses Korean's modifier endings: a present verb takes -는 척하다 (자는 척하다 = pretend to sleep, 일하는 척하다 = pretend to work), an adjective takes -은/-ㄴ 척하다 (아픈 척하다 = pretend to be sick), and a completed action takes -(으)ㄴ 척하다, as in 못 본 척했어 (pretended not to see). A super common real-life line is 상사 와서 일하는 척했어요, which any office worker will recognize. The classic mistake is treating it like -는 것 같다, but those are opposites in spirit: 척하다 is deliberate faking while 것 같다 is an honest impression — so 자는 척하다 (pretending to sleep) is very different from 자는 것 같다 (seems to be sleeping).
